lines: Watch those pointers fade out, one by one. That's the entire cost topic seventeen named, and this topic exists just to get rid of it.
Every entry is about to move directly into the table itself. No node, no next pointer, nothing extra to allocate.
The price for that is hiding in plain sight, and you're about to find it the moment two keys want the same slot.
Here's the whole rule, and it's almost embarrassingly simple: if a slot is full, try the next one.
That's linear probing. One hash function, one fixed step, repeat until you hit something empty.
Simple to compute is not the same thing as fast to run. Keep that tension in mind going into the next two steps.
Two short runs of occupied slots are already sitting there. A new key is about to collide with one of them.
Before I show you what actually happens, predict it yourself. Where does that key probably end up?
answer: Very likely right at the end of one of those runs — making it one slot longer.
Any key whose probe sequence walks into a run has to cross the whole thing before it finds empty space. That's not bad luck, that's the mechanism.

lines: This is primary clustering, and I want you to hear it in the original words: long runs of occupied slots build up, and the long runs tend to get longer.

Notice what's doing the damage here. It isn't a weak hash function, and it isn't bad luck — it's the probing rule itself, the same rule that made linear probing so simple to compute in the first place.
The exact thing that made this mechanism easy to build is the exact thing that makes it slow to run.
Two real answers to that problem, and they work completely differently.
Quadratic probing steps by one, then four, then nine — it jumps away from the run instead of extending it.
Double hashing goes further still. The step itself depends on the key, so two keys that collide at the start don't even follow the same path after that.
Quadratic probing's guarantee comes with real fine print, and I'm not going to let that slide.
It only guarantees you'll find an empty slot within half the table — and only if the table size is prime.
And even with all of that holding, two keys that start at the same slot still follow the exact same sequence after that. That has its own name: secondary clustering.
Here's a correctness trap that catches people who've never hit it before.
You've just deleted the middle entry of this run. Before I show you what real systems do, predict it: can you just empty that slot and move on?
answer: No — a later search walking through that slot would stop the moment it sees empty, and miss every entry sitting just beyond it.
Emptying the slot doesn't just lose the deleted key. It silently breaks every search that used to pass through it on the way to something else.

lines: Two real answers, and they pay completely different costs.
One is a tombstone: a marker that says, out loud, 'nothing here, but keep going.' It keeps that slot occupied forever, until a rehash reclaims it.
The other, the one a real production library actually ships, rehashes every later entry in that same run, immediately, the moment you delete — more work right now, but nothing left behind.
Three load factors, two real strategies, one real measurement each time — nothing here is simulated.
Watch linear probing's average climb fastest as the table fills, while double hashing stays much closer to flat.
That widening gap, right there, is primary clustering actually happening, measured, not just described.
